title: A Guide to Structured Illumination TIRF Microscopy at High Speed with Multiple Colors
protocol: Mark the positions of the components on the optical table.
Separate the objective, lenses L3, L4, and L5, and the SLM each by the sum of their respective focal lengths.
Insert multi-edge dichroic mirror DM4 into the filter cube turret of the microscope frame.
Insert the second dichroic mirror DM3 into a 1" square kinetic mirror mount.
Position dichroic mirror DM3 one focal length away from lens L5.
Accurately define the optical axis for the system before inserting any lenses.
Screw in an alignment tool where the objective lens (OB) was.

Steer a collimated reference beam from Laser 1 through the center of the holes in the two alignment disks using the dichroic mirror DM3 and a temporary alignment mirror at the approximate location of the SLM.
Direct the beam from Laser 1 to the temporary mirror as depicted, using three mirrors and dichroic mirror DM2.
Ensure the temporary mirror at the SLM position is close to perpendicular to the optical axis.
Insert an iris into the beam path before it enters the microscopy body and center it on the beam.
Attach a piece of white card with a small hole centered on the iris.
Reinsert the objective lens (OB).
Center the beam leaving the objective lens on the white card by adjusting its position until a very weak reflection from the back surface of the lens is visible.
Make iterative angular adjustments to the two mirrors (DM3 and alignment mirror at the SLM position) to center the back reflection on the card with the incoming beam.
Temporarily remove the objective lens (OB) and mark the laser spot on the ceiling to create a reference position.
Insert a pair of irises at the height of the reference beam along the threaded holes of the table.
Mount the condenser lens (L5) roughly one focal length away from where the objective will be positioned.
Adjust the position and angle of the condenser lens using a linear translation stage set to translate along the direction of the reference beam.
Ensure that the beam leaving the objective is collimated and hits the reference spot on the ceiling.
Check that the condenser lens is perpendicular to the beam by again checking the back reflection with the iris and white card.
Remove the objective lens (OB) and insert the second lens of the image relay telescope (L4).
Adjust the position and angle of this lens using a linear translation stage to maintain collimation.
Ensure the reference beam still hits the marked spot on the ceiling.
Replace the objective lens (OB) with the first telescope lens (L3).
Adjust the position and angle of L3 to ensure collimation and non-deflection.
Mount the SLM chip on a gimbal mount which allows rotation without translation about the center of the chip surface.
Insert the SLM in place of the mirror.
Adjust the position of the SLM such that the reference beam is at the center of the SLM chip.
Adjust the angle of the SLM to ensure the beam passes through relay lenses (L3 and L4).
Check that the reference beam remains centered on the marked spot after adjustment.
Expand and collimate the reference beam using a Keplerian beam expander.
Mount lenses (L1 and L2) in a cage system for ease of adjustment.
Centre the cage system on the reference beam by removing the lenses and replacing them with irises.
Insert lenses (L1 and L2) back into the cage system.
Adjust the axial position of lens L2 to collimate the expanded beam using a shearing interferometer.
Place lens L2 one focal length away from the surface of the SLM.
Check that the expanded beam remains collimated after passing through relay lenses L3 and L4.
Use a shearing interferometer just after DM3 to check for collimation.
Couple the other two lasers into the beam path using the beam combining dichroic mirrors (DM1 and DM2).
Mount the LCVR with its fast axis at 45° to the incident polarization.
Insert an achromatic half wave plate (HWP) between crossed polarizers.
Rotate the HWP to minimize transmitted power, ensuring perfect 45° alignment of the incident polarization with respect to the LCVR fast axis.
Insert a quarter wave plate (QWP) after the LCVR.
Rotate the QWP to align its slow axis to the incoming polarization by minimizing transmitted power between crossed polarizers.
Position the camera using a stage micrometer slide and transmitted light.
Focus on the reticle using microscope oculars.
Fix the objective lens at the focused position.
Roughly center the camera and move the camera position to bring the image of the reticle into focus by observing the image on screen.
Prepare a monolayer of fluorescent beads by spreading a drop of 100 nm multicolor beads on a #1.5 coverglass.
Leave the bead sample to dry to adsorb the beads to the coverglass and then re-immerse in water.
Place the bead sample onto the objective with immersion oil.
Finely adjust the position of the camera such that the fluorescent bead layer is in focus.
Generate the appropriate SIM binary grating patterns as bitmap files.
Load the SLM control software and click "Connect".
In the "Repertoire" tab, click "Load" to open the repertoire file and check the number of Running Orders contained in the file.
Click "Send to Board" to upload the repertoire file to the SLM.
Wait for the bitmap images to upload and for the device to automatically reboot.
Display a windowed alignment grating on the SLM for the first orientation (for example 0°).
In the SLM control software, select the "Status" tab.
Enter the number of the Running Order (in this case, Running Order "1").
Click "Select" to change the Running Order to the alignment grating.
Insert a spatial mask mounted in an x,y stage into the beam path at the focal position of L3.
Translate the spatial mask's position with respect to the optical axis such that only the desired first orders are passed.
Display the next orientation of the alignment grating and ensure that only the first orders are let through the spatial mask, adjusting its position if required.
Reposition the sample plane by iteratively adjusting the objective lens and camera position.
Adjust the objective position to overlap the two circular beams, bringing the image out of focus.
Reposition the camera to bring the image back into focus.
Fine tune the objective if two circles are still visible.
Repeat this process until the two beams overlap and a single circular region is in focus.
Keep the objective position fixed once the sample plane has been set.
Image a solution of fluorescent dye, for example 10 µM rhodamine 6G for 488 nm excitation wavelength.
Bring the dye sample into focus to confirm TIRF illumination.
Adjust dichroic mirror DM3 if necessary to fine-tune the position of the beams.
Place the bead monolayer sample on the objective and bring into focus.
Program the SLM using its control software to display each of the 3 phase shift images in turn, for the first pattern orientation (0°).
Switch to Running Order 4 of the example repertoire.
Configure the camera using its acquisition software to output two signals: one positive and one negative TTL trigger signal during the global exposure period.
Set Output Trigger Kind 1 and 2 to "Exposure" under "Advanced Camera Properties".
Set Output Trigger Polarity 1 and 2 to "Positive" and "Negative", respectively, in the camera software.
Connect Output 1 and 2 of the camera to the "Trigger" and "Finish" inputs of the SLM using coaxial cables.
Acquire a series of 3 images.
Click "Start" to acquire 3 frames.
Rotate the polarization of the excitation laser with the LCVR using custom software to achieve azimuthal polarization and therefore the highest modulation contrast for the given pattern orientation.
Load the LCVR calibration software.
Enter 0 and 8 for the Minimum and Maximum Voltage respectively.
Click "Sweep LCVR Voltage" to rotate the polarization.
Wait for the calibration process to complete, and note down the measured voltage.
Repeat this calibration process for the remaining two pattern orientations (60° and 120°).
Repeat the calibration process for each of the excitation wavelengths.
Synchronize the camera exposure with the LCVR, lasers, emission filter wheel, and piezo z-stage.
Use a high speed data acquisition (DAQ) board as the master clock source for the system.
Modulate the lasers using the SLM's LED Enable output signal.
Determine the axial chromatic aberration offset experimentally by focusing on a multicolor bead monolayer sample at the first wavelength, then switching to the second wavelength.
Refocus the beads and measure the change in z position that was needed after changing wavelengths.
Apply the determined z-offset to the piezo z-stage every time the excitation wavelength is changed.
Switch the SLM Running Order to a full series of 9 binary grating images required for TIRF-SIM using the SLM control software.
Acquire 9 images of the bead sample using the camera control software.
Select "Hard Disk Record" as the scan type in the "Sequence" pane of the camera software.
Change the frame count to 9.
Click "Start" to acquire images.
Save acquired images as TIFF files.
Reconstruct a super-resolution image from raw TIFF images using commercial or custom software to validate resolution improvement over standard TIRF.
